fields.Front: Define throughput and distinguish instantaneous from average throughput.
fields.Back:
Throughput: the rate (bits per unit time) at which bits are delivered from sender to receiver.
Instantaneous: the rate at a given instant (the fluctuating number in a download dialog).
Average: rate over a longer period; F bits delivered in T seconds gives F/T bits/s.

fields.Front: Using the pipe/fluid model with server link Rs and client link Rc, what is the end-to-end throughput when Rs < Rc and when Rs > Rc?
fields.Back:
Rs < Rc: the client pipe carries bits as fast as they arrive, so throughput = Rs.
Rs > Rc: the client pipe cannot keep up; bits leave at Rc and a backlog builds before the narrow pipe, so throughput = Rc.
Either way throughput = min(Rs, Rc): the bottleneck link.

fields.Front: Numeric: (a) a 32 Mbit file with server link Rs = 2 Mbps and client link Rc = 1 Mbps; (b) a 40 Mbit file with a 10 Mbps server access link and a 4 Mbps client access link, uncongested core. Throughput and transfer time?
fields.Back:
(a) throughput = min(2, 1) = 1 Mbps (client access link is the bottleneck); T = 32 x 10^6 / 10^6 = 32 s.
(b) throughput = min(10, 4) = 4 Mbps; T = 40 x 10^6 / (4 x 10^6) = 10 s.

fields.Front: Numeric: 10 server-client connections share one backbone link. (a) Slide numbers: R = 6 bps, Rs = 2 bps, Rc = 3 bps. (b) R = 100 Mbps, Rs = 20 Mbps, Rc = 5 Mbps. Per-connection throughput and bottleneck in each?
fields.Back:
Per-connection throughput = min(Rc, Rs, R/10).
(a) min(3, 2, 0.6) = 0.6 bps - the shared core link is the bottleneck.
(b) min(5, 20, 10) = 5 Mbps - the client access link is the bottleneck, as is typical in practice since the real core is over-provisioned.

fields.Front: Why is 'bandwidth' not the same as 'throughput'?
fields.Back:
Bandwidth (transmission rate R) is a property of one link.
Throughput is end-to-end: limited by the bottleneck link on the path and by how a shared link is divided among connections (fair share R/n).
A 1 Gbps access link gives nothing beyond a 4 Mbps bottleneck elsewhere.

fields.Front: Textbook only: what is the bandwidth-delay product, and what does R = 5 Mbps over 20,000 km at s = 2.5 x 10^8 m/s give? (Kurose §1.4, P25)
fields.Back:
The bandwidth-delay product R x d_prop is the maximum number of bits that can be 'in flight' on a link at one instant - bits the sender has pushed out but the receiver has not yet seen. Picture the link as a pipe: the product is its volume.
d_prop = 2 x 10^7 m / (2.5 x 10^8 m/s) = 0.08 s = 80 ms.
R x d_prop = 5 x 10^6 x 0.08 = 400,000 bits in the link at once.
Related: the width of one bit is s / R = 2.5 x 10^8 / 5 x 10^6 = 50 m, longer than a football field. This is the idea behind TCP window sizing in Chapter 3.

fields.Text: End-to-end throughput over links Rs and Rc is {{c1::min(Rs, Rc)}}, the rate of the {{c1::bottleneck link}} (the link that constrains end-to-end throughput); over N links in series it is {{c1::min(R1, ..., RN)}} and F bits take about {{c1::F / min(R1..RN)}} seconds.

With 10 connections fairly sharing a backbone link R, per-connection throughput = {{c1::min(Rc, Rs, R/10)}}; in practice the {{c1::access links (Rc or Rs)}} are usually the bottleneck because the core is {{c1::over-provisioned}}.
